newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian credit policy seen boosting commodities.
newsitem.headline: Indian credit policy seen boosting commodities.

text.p: India's decision to scrap its archaic credit controls on key commodities, including sugar, cotton and oilseeds, will boost trading volumes, production and prices, analysts said on Sunday.
"The move is unprecedented and a radical departure from the past," said commodities' analyst C.S. Aiyar. "It's a crucial step in the process of India's economic liberalisation."

The removal of the decades-old credit controls on commodities was among a number of measures announced by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Saturday in its credit policy statement for the second half of 1996/97 (April/March).
The central bank exempted oilseeds and oils, sugar, cotton, pulses and coarse foodgrains from selective credit controls with effect from October 21 following an improved supply of these commodities.
An excellent monsoon this year has brightened India's prospects of a bumper harvest in most crops. Sugar cane, oilseeds and cotton crops are reported to be good.
Aiyar said the RBI had in the past only marginally tinkered with its credit controls, designed mainly to discourage hoarding of sensitive essential commodities.
"Supplies are likely to be good. There's no incentive to hoard because imports are also allowed freely under economic reforms," said Aiyar.
Traders said at present industry and trade dealing in commodities were compelled to keep heavy margins of up to 40 percent against advances from banks.
"Nowhere in the world are industry and trade being subject to such heavy margins," said Navin Shah, president of Bombay Oilseeds and Oils Exchange.
Shah said industry and trade had not been getting enough money to improve production and to expand business.
"The removal of credit controls will help boost trading volumes, production and prices," he said. "It's good for the economy as a whole."
"Production in the oilseeds crushing industry will improve, and so will the supply of oil. There's enough demand to keep prices at remunerative levels to help farmers," Shah said.

India is expected to harvest about 22 million tonnes of oilseeds in 1996/97 (November/October), the same as during the past year. Its edible oil imports, mostly palm olein, may double to one million tonnes from the previous year's 500,000 tonnes.
The RBI also exempted imported oilseeds and edible oils from credit controls.
Shah said he would expect the government to allow futures trading in commodities, yet another crucial and much-awaited step in the process of market reforms.
Sugar traders said removal of controls would help sugar mills clear their piling arrears with cane growers.
"Sugar mills are burdened with a lot of production and high inventories. Easing of credit controls will help them," said Bombay Sugar Merchants' Association president Mohan Gurnani.
India's sugar production in 1996/97 (October/September) is expected to be around 15 million tonnes, slightly lower than 15.45 million harvested in the previous year.
Cotton traders, who expect a bumper crop of 16 million bales (one bale is 170 kgs) in 1996/97 (October/September), about the same as in the previous year, welcomed the RBI move.
"The season has just begun. We are happy that enough funds will be available to trade," said a cotton dealer.
